Look up any contest problem from our 320-problem research corpus by its canonical ID (`#001`–`#256` or `R-01`–`R-64`), judge code (`AtCoder`, `Codeforces`, `Luogu`, `LOJ`, `UOJ`, `POJ`, `QOJ`, `UVA`, `SPOJ`, `CSES`), or modelling archetype, and jump directly to the chapter or blind checkpoint where its **4-Step English-to-Graph Compilation** is derived.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to Use This Master Archive Without Spoiling Blind Diagnosis

1. **Practice Diagnosis Before Reading the Chapter Link**: If you encounter an unfamiliar contest problem in the wild, do **not** immediately read the **Primary Modelling Archetype** column in Section 2. Instead, open the **Judge Reverse-Lookup Index (Section 6)**, locate the Part (`Part I`–`Part VI`) to which the problem belongs, and attempt the corresponding **Blind Checkpoint (`CP-I`–`CP-VI`)** diagnostic flowchart first.
2. **Audit Your Broken Gadgets Against `FM-01`–`FM-25`**: Every accepted problem in Section 2 is cross-tagged with its primary **Failure Mode (`FM-xx`)**—the exact mathematical bug (such as omitting reverse $\infty$-edges in unary chains, applying Bipartite Variable Inversion on a graph with odd cycles, or splitting a concave edge cost into parallel arcs) that causes naive translations to fail.
3. **Understand Why Famous Classics Were Quarantined (Sections 4 & 5)**: In adherence to our **No Boilerplate / Zero Magic Gadgets** mandate, 64 problems (`R-01`–`R-64`) were quarantined from the main chapter ladders. Section 4 documents every quarantined problem—whether it is a bare solver template (`P3376`, `P3381`), a structural duplicate, an NP-hard concave/3D-matching trap, or a famous **non-flow lookalike** from the Chinese *"24 Network Flow Problems"* (`网络流 24 题`)—and routes you to its rigorous non-template replacement.
:::

## 1. Architecture of the 320-Problem Corpus

Across Phase 1 research (`Wave 1A`–`Wave 1D`), our team harvested **320 problems** from English (`Codeforces`, `ICPC World Finals`, `TopCoder`, `USACO`, `POJ`, `UVA`, `CSES`), Chinese (`Luogu`, `LOJ`, `UOJ`, `QOJ`, `NOI`, `CTSC`, `WC`, `SDOI`, `ZJOI`, `HNOI`, `国家集训队论文`, `网络流 24 题`), and Japanese (`AtCoder AGC/ARC/ABC`, `yukicoder`, `燃やす埋める` treatises) sources. Every single problem is accounted for in a strict bijective partition:

$$
320 \text{ Total Problems} \;=\; \underbrace{192 \text{ Chapter Ladder Problems}}_{\text{24 Chapters } \times \text{ 8 Problems } (\#001\text{--}\#192)} \;+\; \underbrace{48 \text{ Blind Checkpoint Problems}}_{\text{6 Checkpoints } \times \text{ 8 Problems } (\#193\text{--}\#240)} \;+\; \underbrace{16 \text{ Grand Synthesis Problems}}_{\text{Capstone I } (\#241\text{--}\#256)} \;+\; \underbrace{64 \text{ Quarantined Problems}}_{\text{Templates, Duplicates \& Decoys } (\text{R-01--R-64})}
$$

### 1.2 Difficulty Tier Calibration (`SS` / `Int` / `Adv` / `Mas`)

Every chapter ladder (`Ch 01`–`Ch 24`) contains exactly **8 curated problems** ordered strictly across four calibrated difficulty tiers:

- **`SS` — Stepping Stone (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints)**: Clean, canonical non-template problems that isolate a single modelling transformation (e.g., translating a 2D grid conflict into parity bipartite MIS, or differencing a linear inequality system into conservation equations). Typical rating: `CF 1700–2000` / `AtCoder ABC-F,G` / `Luogu 提高+/省选-`.
- **`Int` — Intermediate (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints)**: Requires combining the chapter's core transformation with a secondary structural invariant (e.g., binary search on bottlenecks, residual SCC edge classification, or Tarjan topological pruning before project selection). Typical rating: `CF 2100–2400` / `AtCoder ARC-E,F` / `Luogu 省选/NOI-`.
- **`Adv` — Advanced (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints)**: Non-obvious algebraic compilation where the problem statement contains **zero graph terminology**, or requires rescuing a broken submodularity/convexity condition via variable inversion, complement counting, or persistent data structures. Typical rating: `CF 2500–2800` / `AtCoder AGC-C,D,E` / `NOI / Provincial Selection`.
- **`Mas` — Mastery (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints + 16 Synthesis)**: Research-grade or Olympiad flagship benchmarks (`CF 2900–3500`, `AtCoder AGC-F`, `ICPC World Finals`, `NOI / CTSC / WC`) requiring multi-layer compilation, continuous Coarea decomposition, simulated MCMF on trees/segment trees, or $L_p$ Isotonic Regression.

### 1.3 Master Failure Mode Taxonomy (`FM-01` to `FM-25`)

Throughout the textbook, every gadget construction is paired with an explicit **Broken Gadget Counterexample**. The table below indexes all 25 canonical failure modes referenced across Sections 2–5:

| Code | Failure Mode Name | What Goes Wrong in the Naive Graph / Algorithm | Canonical Fix & Home Chapter |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`FM-01`** | **Directed vs. Undirected Residual Trap** | Adding an undirected edge $\{u,v\}$ of capacity $c$ as two independent directed arcs without shared residual coupling, or setting reverse capacity to $0$ instead of $c$. | Couple $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$ in the residual pair (`e` and `e^1`), initializing both forward capacities to $c$ ([Ch 01](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd)). |
| **`FM-02`** | **Greedy / Naive "$S$-Reachable = All Min-Cut" Fallacy** | Assuming every edge crossing from the $S$-reachable residual set $R_S$ to $V \setminus R_S$ is mandatory in *every* minimum cut, or that any saturated edge is a cut edge. | Run Tarjan SCC on $G_f$: $(u,v)$ is in *some* min-cut iff $f(u,v)=c(u,v)$ and $\text{scc}(u) \neq \text{scc}(v)$; in *all* min-cuts iff $\text{scc}(u)=\text{scc}(S)$ and $\text{scc}(v)=\text{scc}(T)$ ([Ch 02](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd)). |
| **`FM-03`** | **Un-Split Vertex / Two-Commodity Merging Trap** | Placing vertex capacity on incident edges, or testing two-commodity routing by only checking $S_1 \to T_1, S_2 \to T_2$ without testing the swapped $S_1 \to T_2, S_2 \to T_1$ run. | Split $v \to (v_{\text{in}}, v_{\text{out}})$ ([Ch 03](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd)); run second max-flow with $S_2 \leftrightarrow T_2$ swapped (`[CQOI2014] 危桥`, [Ch 02](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd)). |
| **`FM-04`** | **Missing Companion Edge $(t, s, \infty)$ in Lower-Bound Flow** | Running max-flow from $S^*$ to $T^*$ in a lower-bound $s$-$t$ network without adding the feedback arc $(t, s, \infty)$, violating conservation at $s$ and $t$. | Add $(t, s, \infty)$ to convert $s$-$t$ flow into a closed circulation before saturating $S^* \to T^*$ ([Ch 04](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd)). |
| **`FM-05`** | **König Duality on Non-Bipartite Graphs (Odd-Cycle Trap)** | Applying $\text{MVC} = \text{MaxMatching}$ or $\text{MIS} = |V| - \text{MaxMatching}$ to a graph containing an odd cycle $C_{2k+1}$, where $\text{MVC} > \nu(G)$. | Verify bipartiteness first, or pass to the complement of a two-clique graph / use general Blossom matching ([Ch 05](../chapters/ch05-bipartite-matching-konig-mvc-mis.qmd), [Ch 22](../chapters/ch22-ds-accelerated-flow-graphs-blossom-matching.qmd)). |
| **`FM-06`** | **Un-Reset Visited Array in Alternating-Path Game Simulation** | Failing to unmatch or update Dulmage–Mendelsohn status dynamically as multi-move grid games progress (`[NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋`). | Treat each move as moving the blank token along an alternating path and re-test augmenting paths from the current vertex after deleting the previous node ([Ch 06](../chapters/ch06-grid-parity-dulmage-mendelsohn-games.qmd)). |
| **`FM-07`** | **Unreachable Positive-Weight Cycles in Project Selection** | Feeding a dependency graph with directed cycles (or nodes reachable from cycles) directly into a closure min-cut (`[NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸`), allowing the solver to "buy" mutually deadlocked positive-weight nodes. | Prune all vertices with in-degree $>0$ after Kahn's topological sort on the prerequisite graph before building the closure network ([Ch 09](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd)). |
| **`FM-08`** | **Submodularity Violation ($A + D > B + C$) on Un-Flipped Graphs** | Attempting to compile a pairwise reward/penalty table with $A + D > B + C$ directly into $s$-$t$ cut arcs, producing negative edge capacities $c_{uv} < 0$. | Check if the interaction graph is bipartite; if so, apply **Bipartite Variable Inversion** $y_v = 1 - x_v$ on one side to negate the cross-difference into $B+C-A-D \ge 0$ ([Ch 10](../chapters/ch10-pseudo-boolean-cuts-submodularity-burn-bury.qmd), [Ch 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd)). |
| **`FM-09`** | **Odd-Cycle Collision in Bipartite Variable Inversion** | Attempting to rescue a supermodular penalty ($A+D > B+C$) when the conflict graph contains an odd cycle (e.g., a triangle of "same-color bonus" edges). | Recognize that same-state penalties on non-bipartite graphs are NP-hard (Max-Cut); either reformulate via complement / line graph or dualize if planar ([Ch 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd)). |
| **`FM-10`** | **Missing Reverse $\infty$-Constraint Arcs in Multi-State Chains** | Omitting the backward $(z_{i,t}, z_{i,t-1}, \infty)$ monotonicity arcs in a unary chain (`[HNOI2013] 切糕`), allowing an $s$-$t$ cut to sever multiple edges of the same variable and create fractured indicator states $z_{i,1}=0, z_{i,2}=1$. | Always wire $(v_{i,t}, v_{i,t-1}, \infty)$ so any finite cut intersects each variable's chain in **at most one** transition edge ([Ch 12](../chapters/ch12-multi-state-unary-chains-threshold-cuts.qmd)). |
| **`FM-11`** | **Non-Convex Interaction Function in Ishikawa / Coarea Compilation** | Applying the Ishikawa cross-edge formula $w = \frac{1}{2}\Delta_i \Delta_j g < 0$ when $g(a_i - a_j)$ is concave rather than convex, producing negative capacities. | Verify discrete convexity $g(d+1) - 2g(d) + g(d-1) \ge 0$ before compiling cross-edges ([Ch 13](../chapters/ch13-ishikawa-convex-penalties-coarea-parametric-cuts.qmd)). |
| **`FM-12`** | **Empty-Subgraph ($S' = \emptyset$) Zero-Cut Trap in Density Subgraph** | Formulating $\max |E(S')|/|S'|$ as a standard closure cut without shifting by a large constant $U$, where the trivial cut $S' = \emptyset$ has cost $0$ and masks whether a positive-excess non-empty subgraph exists. | Use the shifted degree-Regularization cut or enforce $|S'| \ge 1$ via binary search validation ([Ch 14](../chapters/ch14-fractional-programming-maximum-density-subgraphs.qmd)). |
| **`FM-13`** | **Un-Split Exterior Face in Planar $s$-$t$ Dual Shortest Path** | Dualizing a planar graph into faces when $s$ and $t$ do not both lie on the outer boundary face, or forgetting to split the outer face into $F_{\text{top}}$ and $F_{\text{bottom}}$ along the $(t \to s)$虛arc. | Embed $s, t$ on the outer boundary, add virtual arc $(t,s)$, and split the unbounded face into $S^*$ and $T^*$ ([Ch 15](../chapters/ch15-planar-cycle-cut-duality-shortest-paths.qmd)). |
| **`FM-14`** | **Adding Residual Edges Instead of Rebuilding in Gomory–Hu Gusfield** | Running Gusfield's $N-1$ max-flows on the *modified* residual graph from the previous iteration instead of resetting flow values to zero before each pair. | Reset all edge flows to $0$ before each of the $N-1$ $s$-$t$ max-flow calls ([Ch 16](../chapters/ch16-mincut-dp-global-mincut-gomory-hu-trees.qmd)). |
| **`FM-15`** | **Un-Initialized Negative Costs in Dijkstra SSP without Johnson Potentials** | Running Dijkstra directly on an MCMF network with initial negative-cost edges, or failing to saturate negative-cost edges / cycles via lower-bound initialization. | Compute initial potentials $\pi$ via Bellman–Ford/DAG DP, or pre-saturate negative-cost arcs $(u,v,c,w<0)$ and balance excesses via $S^* \to T^*$ ([Ch 17](../chapters/ch17-mcmf-foundations-potentials-slope-negative-cycles.qmd)). |
| **`FM-16`** | **Concave Edge Cost Splitting / Zero-Length Vertical Segment Loop** | Splitting a concave cost function ($\Delta c_1 > \Delta c_2$) into parallel arcs (where MCMF greedily picks the second unit before the first!), or adding a zero-length interval $[x, x]$ with $w > 0$ (`最长k可重线段集`) creating a positive-weight self-loop. | Only convex costs split into parallel arcs; for vertical segments $x_1 = x_2$, double coordinates $x \gets 2x$ and map vertical segments to $[2x, 2x+1]$ vs. open intervals $(2x_1, 2x_2)$ ([Ch 18](../chapters/ch18-convex-marginal-splitting-degree-penalties-tournaments.qmd), [Ch 19](../chapters/ch19-k-interval-coverage-equation-difference-method.qmd)). |
| **`FM-17`** | **Sign Inversion in Consecutive Equation Differencing ($\Delta_i = E_i - E_{i-1}$)** | Getting the orientation of slack variables $s_i \ge 0$ or interval variables $x_j$ backwards when subtracting consecutive linear equations $E_i - E_{i-1}$. | Strictly enforce conservation $\sum_{\text{in}} - \sum_{\text{out}} = b_i - b_{i-1}$: an interval covering $[l_j, r_j]$ enters at $+x_j$ in $\Delta_{l_j}$ and exits at $-x_j$ in $\Delta_{r_j+1}$, hence forms an arc $r_j+1 \to l_j$ (or $l_j \to r_j+1$ under reversed sign convention) ([Ch 19](../chapters/ch19-k-interval-coverage-equation-difference-method.qmd)). |
| **`FM-18`** | **Upfront $O(NM^2)$ Graph Materialization in Dynamic Scheduling** | Building all $M \times P$ chef-position vertices and $N \times M \times P$ edges before running MCMF (`[NOI2012] 美食节`), causing TLE during SPFA/Dijkstra scans. | Materialize only the *first* reverse-position slot $(j, 1)$ per chef initially; dynamically spawn $(j, k+1)$ only after the augmenting path saturates $(j, k)$ ([Ch 20](../chapters/ch20-cycle-covers-dynamic-scheduling-resource-reuse-hubs.qmd)). |
| **`FM-19`** | **Contaminated vs. Clean Resource Confusion in Napkin Reuse** | Allowing "dirty" resources at day $i_{\text{out}}$ to flow directly to "clean" demand at day $(i+1)_{\text{in}}$ without passing through a wash delay edge (`餐巾计划问题`). | Separate each day into `dirty supply` ($S \to i_{\text{dirty}}$) and `clean demand` ($i_{\text{clean}} \to T$); only dirty nodes can postpone for free ($i_{\text{dirty}} \to (i+1)_{\text{dirty}}$) or wash ($i_{\text{dirty}} \to (i+d)_{\text{clean}}$) ([Ch 20](../chapters/ch20-cycle-covers-dynamic-scheduling-resource-reuse-hubs.qmd)). |
| **`FM-20`** | **Missing Regret Push (`反悔边`) in Simulated MCMF Heaps** | Pushing only the raw item cost into a greedy heap without pushing the residual cancellation cost $2\text{val}_{\text{chosen}} - \text{val}_{\text{prev}}$ after matching (`Buy Low Sell High`, `CF 802 O`). | Maintain the exact residual cycle invariant: every match $(u, v)$ must insert the reverse residual marginal cost into the opposite priority queue ([Ch 23](../chapters/ch23-simulated-mcmf-regret-greedy-heap-segtree.qmd)). |
| **`FM-21`** | **Shared Mutable Nodes Across Versions in Persistent Segment Tree Flow** | Linking historical prefix queries directly to an in-place mutated segment tree (`BZOJ 3218`), allowing flow from time $t$ to leak backward and reach targets inserted at time $t' > t$. | Allocate new persistent tree nodes along the updated path at step $i$, linking $\text{new\_node} \to \text{old\_node}$ with capacity $\infty$ so flow only travels to earlier indices $j < i$ ([Ch 22](../chapters/ch22-ds-accelerated-flow-graphs-blossom-matching.qmd)). |
| **`FM-22`** | **Bipartite Assumption on Odd-Cycle General Matching Graphs** | Running Hopcroft–Karp or Dinic on a general matching problem (`[WC2016] 挑战 NPC`, `CF 1089 B`), where odd alternating cycles cause augmenting paths to self-intersect. | Contract odd cycles via Edmonds' Blossom algorithm (`带花树`) or test algebraic rank via the skew-symmetric Tutte matrix ([Ch 22](../chapters/ch22-ds-accelerated-flow-graphs-blossom-matching.qmd)). |
| **`FM-23`** | **Incomplete 5-Queue Cross-Cancel Transitions in Bipartite Simulated Flow** | Maintaining only direct match heaps when simulating a $K$-bounded common-element constraint (`[NOI2019] 序列`), missing the 3-hop augmenting paths that free a shared slot by swapping an already-paired element. | Enumerate all elementary augmenting path types in the constant-size residual gadget and maintain a dedicated priority queue for each valid state transition ([Ch 23](../chapters/ch23-simulated-mcmf-regret-greedy-heap-segtree.qmd)). |
| **`FM-24`** | **Non-Convex or Discontinuous Derivative Split in $L_p$ Isotonic Regression** | Attempting to binary search a single threshold $[f_i > \text{mid}]$ for $L_p$ Isotonic Regression when the node weight functions $w_i(x)$ are non-convex, violating the nested cut-tree monotonicity property. | Ensure each penalty $w_i(x)$ is convex so its discrete derivative $w_i(\text{mid}+\epsilon) - w_i(\text{mid})$ is monotone in $\text{mid}$, enabling Divide-and-Conquer + Closure Min-Cut ([Ch 24](../chapters/ch24-isotonic-regression-matroid-intersection-synthesis.qmd)). |
| **`FM-25`** | **Forcing Network Flow Onto a Non-Flow Lookalike Problem** | Building an exponential or malformed flow network for a problem that lacks flow conservation or submodularity—such as bitmask shortest paths (`孤岛营救`), DAG DP, or greedy exchange—simply because it appeared in `网络流 24 题`. | Audit conservation and TU/submodularity first; see the **Non-Flow Decoys** in Sections 4 and 5 ([CP-I](../checkpoints/cp01-part1-foundations.qmd)–[CP-VI](../checkpoints/cp06-part6-ds-blossom-simulated-isotonic.qmd)). |

## 2. Complete Master Index of Accepted Problems (`#001`–`#256`)

This section provides the complete bijective directory of all **256 accepted non-template problems**, organized by textbook chapter (`#001`–`#192`), blind checkpoint (`#193`–`#240`), and grand synthesis reserve (`#241`–`#256`).

### 2.1 Part I: Flow Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Time-Layered DAGs & Circulations (`#001`–`#032`)

#### [Chapter 1 — Flow Conservation, Residual Networks & Max-Flow Min-Cut](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd) (`#001`–`#008`)

| ID | Tier | Problem & Judge Code | Primary Modelling Archetype | Diagnostic Trigger & Key Constraint | Failure Mode |
| :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **`#001`** | `SS` | **SGU 326 / CF Gym** — *Perspective* (alt: **Luogu P2756** *飞行员配对方案*) | Elimination Feasibility via Remaining Game Allocation | Sports league: fix team 1's max wins $W_1$; check if remaining match points can be distributed without any team $i$ exceeding $W_1$. | `FM-01` |
| **`#002`** | `SS` | **CF 546 E** — *Soldier and Traveling* (alt: **Luogu P3254** *圆桌问题*) | 1-Step Bipartite Conservation & Flow Reconstruction | $N \le 100$: soldiers move at most 1 edge from $a_i$ to $b_i$; check $\sum a_i = \sum b_i = \text{MaxFlow}$ and print adjacency matrix $f(u, v')$. | `FM-01` |
| **`#003`** | `Int` | **CF 653 D** — *Delivery Bears* (alt: **Luogu P2763** *试题库问题*) | Binary Search on Unit Weight + Scaled Integer Capacity | $X \le 10^5$ bears move along $s \to t$ paths carrying equal weight $w$; binary search $w$ and assign capacity $\lfloor c_e / w \rfloor$. | `FM-01` |
| **`#004`** | `Int` | **CF 498 C** — *Array and Operations* | Prime-Factor Decoupled Bipartite Matching Flow | Array $a_1, \dots, a_n$ ($n \le 100$) with good pairs $(i, j)$ of opposite parity ($i+j$ odd); decouple by each prime $p \mid a_i$ into independent flow runs. | `FM-05` |
| **`#005`** | `Adv` | **POJ 3498 / UVA 12125** — *March of the Penguins* | Enumerating Sink + Vertex-Capacity Splitting | $N \le 100$ ice floes with jump limit $b_i$; split $i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{b_i} i_{\text{out}}$ and test all $N$ floes as the meeting sink $T$. | `FM-03` |
| **`#006`** | `Adv` | **AtCoder ABC 239 G** — *Builder Takahashi* | Minimum-Weight Vertex Cut & $S$-Reachable Reconstruction | Undirected graph $N \le 100$ with vertex removal costs $c_i$; split $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_v} v_{\text{out}}$ and extract $v_{\text{in}} \in R_S, v_{\text{out}} \notin R_S$. | `FM-02`, `FM-03` |
| **`#007`** | `Mas` | **CF 510 E** — *Fox And Dinner* | Parity Bipartite Degree-2 Factor & Cycle Extraction | Arrange $N \le 200$ integers into circular tables where adjacent sums $a_i + a_j$ are prime; odd+even $= \text{odd prime}$ forces bipartite degree-2 flow $= N$. | `FM-05` |
| **`#008`** | `Mas` | **CF 1383 F** — *Special Edges* | $2^K$ Dynamic Residual Rollback + Gray-Code DFS | $K \le 10$ special edges with $Q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ capacity queries; precompute base max-flow once and maintain $2^K$ residual states in $O(2^K m)$ via FF augmentations. | `FM-01` |

#### [Chapter 2 — Residual Graph Anatomy, Cut-Edge Classification & Rollback](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd) (`#009`–`#016`)

| ID | Tier | Problem & Judge Code | Primary Modelling Archetype | Diagnostic Trigger & Key Constraint | Failure Mode |

## 3. The Four Flagship Benchmarks & Non-Graph-to-Flow Recognition Matrix

### 3.1 Deep-Dive Cross-Reference: The Four User-Highlighted Flagship Benchmarks

These four flagship problems represent the pinnacle of modern non-graph-to-cut compilation. Each appears in its home chapter in Part III **and** in the cross-paradigm synthesis comparison in [Capstone I](synthesis-reserve.qmd):

| Flagship Benchmark | Canonical ID & Home Chapter | Non-Graph English Surface Statement | Why DP / Greedy Fails | Key Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation Breakthrough |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. AtCoder AGC 038 F**<br>*Two Permutations* | **`#087`** ([Ch 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd)) & `Syn-03` ([Capstone I](synthesis-reserve.qmd)) | Given two permutations $P, Q$ of $\{0..N-1\}$ ($N \le 10^5$), form $A_i \in \{i, P_i\}$ and $B_i \in \{i, Q_i\}$ so $A, B$ are valid permutations maximizing $|\{i : A_i \neq B_i\}|$. | $P$-cycles and $Q$-cycles intersect arbitrarily, creating a general bipartite hypergraph of cycle-shift decisions with no treewidth bound. | 1. **Cycle Locking**: Every cycle $c$ of $P$ has a single binary state $x_c \in \{0,1\}$ ($A_i = i$ vs. $A_i = P_i$).<br>2. **Bipartite Variable Inversion**: Flip $Q$-cycle indicators $y_d = 1 - x'_d$ so the 5 collision cases ($i = P_i = Q_i$, $P_i = Q_i \neq i$, etc.) all compile into submodular $x_c(1-y_d)$ and $y_d(1-x_c)$ cut edges! |
| **2. AtCoder ARC 107 F**<br>*Sum of Abs* | **`#095`** ([Ch 12](../chapters/ch12-multi-state-unary-chains-threshold-cuts.qmd)) & `Syn-04` ([Capstone I](synthesis-reserve.qmd)) | Delete a subset of vertices (paying $A_v$) so remaining connected components $C$ maximize $\sum_C |\sum_{v \in C} B_v|$ ($N, M \le 300$). | Absolute value $|\sum_{v \in C} B_v|$ depends globally on component connectivity; general graphs cannot be solved by tree DP. | 1. **Linearizing $|X|$**: Replace $|\sum_{v \in C} B_v|$ by choosing a uniform sign $\sigma_v \in \{+1, -1\}$ for every vertex in $C$.<br>2. **3-State Split Chain**: Assign each vertex $v$ state $\sigma_v \in \{+1, 0 (\text{deleted}), -1\}$ via a 2-node split $(v_{\text{in}}, v_{\text{out}})$, and forbid $+1$ adjacent to $-1$ via $u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{out}}$ and $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}$! |
| **3. AtCoder ARC 142 E**<br>*Pairing Wizards* | **`#096`** ([Ch 12](../chapters/ch12-multi-state-unary-chains-threshold-cuts.qmd)) & `Syn-05` ([Capstone I](synthesis-reserve.qmd)) | Increment $a_i$ (+1 costs 1) so every pair $(u,v)$ satisfies $\min(a_u,a_v) \ge \min(b_u,b_v)$ and $\max(a_u,a_v) \ge \max(b_u,b_v)$ ($N \le 100, b_i \le 100$). | $\max(a_u, a_v) \ge B$ is a logical **OR** constraint ($a_u \ge B \lor a_v \ge B$), which on a general graph is NP-hard Vertex Cover! | 1. **Deterministic Floor**: Force $a_u \gets \max(a_u, \min(b_u,b_v))$ immediately.<br>2. **Hidden Bipartiteness**: After floor raising, if $\max(a_u,a_v) < B = \max(b_u,b_v)$, one endpoint has $a_u \ge b_u$ ("satisfied") and the other has $a_v < b_v < B$ ("unsatisfied"). Thus all OR-edges strictly cross between two disjoint vertex sets $V_{\text{sat}}$ and $V_{\text{unsat}}$! |
| **4. Codeforces 1427 G**<br>*One Billion Shades of Grey* | **`#103`** ([Ch 13](../chapters/ch13-ishikawa-convex-penalties-coarea-parametric-cuts.qmd)) & `Syn-06` ([Capstone I](synthesis-reserve.qmd)) | Fill interior cells of an $N \times N$ grid ($N \le 200$) with fixed border values $\le 10^9$ to minimize $\sum_{(u,v) \in E} |x_u - x_v|$. | Value domain $V_{\max} = 10^9$ makes unary chains ($200^2 \times 10^9$ vertices) impossible by 7 orders of magnitude. | 1. **Coarea Decomposition**: $\sum |x_u - x_v| = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \sum |[x_u > \lambda] - [x_v > \lambda]| d\lambda$, which is constant on each interval $(v_k, v_{k+1})$ between sorted boundary values.<br>2. **Parametric Rollback**: Sweep $\lambda$ across $4N$ boundary values, flipping one border tile from $S$ to $T$ by un-pushing $\le 4$ units of flow and re-augmenting in $O(N^3)$ total! |

### 3.2 The Non-Graph-to-Flow Recognition Matrix

One of the hardest skills in competitive programming is recognizing a flow or min-cut problem when the English problem statement contains **zero graph terminology**. The table below indexes all major non-graph problem domains in our archive and shows how their algebraic structures compile into flow networks:

| Non-Graph Surface Domain | Tell-Tale Algebraic / Combinatorial Clues | Canonical Archive Problems (`#001`–`#256`) | Target Compilation Paradigm |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Permutations & Cycles** | Choosing between $A_i = i$ and $A_i = P_i$; swapping elements in two permutations $P, Q$; bounding frequency $cnt_v$ of values in $[L_i, R_i]$. | **`#087`** (*AGC 038 F*), **`#056`** (*CF 1783 F Double Sort II*), **`#137`** (*CF 863 F Almost Permutation*), **`#094`** (*CF 1662 J*) | Cycle-level indicator variables + Bipartite Variable Inversion ([Ch 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd)), or Cycle-Intersection MVC ([Ch 07](../chapters/ch07-birkhoff-von-neumann-row-col-edge-coloring.qmd)). |
| **Number Theory (Primes, Divisibility, XOR)** | Pair conflicts when $a_i + a_j = \text{prime}$ (odd + even!); divisibility implication $i \mid j \implies x_i \le x_j$; bitwise XOR edge sum $\sum (a_u \oplus a_v)$; ratio $a_i/a_j = p$ ($\Omega(a_i)$ parity). | **`#004`** (*CF 498 C*), **`#007`** (*CF 510 E*), **`#037`** (*CF 808 F*), **`#058`** (*P2765 魔术球*), **`#068`** (*ARC 085 E MUL*), **`#079`** (*CF 1473 F*), **`#100`** (*BZOJ 2400*), **`#164`** (*P4068*) | Parity bipartite split ($\text{odd}+\text{even}=\text{odd prime}$, [Ch 05](../chapters/ch05-bipartite-matching-konig-mvc-mis.qmd)), or Divisibility Poset Closure ([Ch 09](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd)). |
| **Linear Algebra & Matrices** | Bilinear form $\max (x B x^T - x C)$; real matrix rounding preserving row/col sums; 2D XOR suffix flips; linear basis replacement $a_i \preceq b_j$. | **`#071`** (*P3973 线性代数*), **`#026`** (*POJ 2396*), **`#032`** (*BZOJ 3698*), **`#049`** (*P1129*), **`#055`** (*CF 1592 F1*), **`#176`** (*Tutte Matrix*), **`#189`** (*P6621 魔法商店*) | Quadratic-to-Closure reduction ([Ch 09](../chapters/ch09-maximum-weight-closure-project-selection.qmd)), Lower-Bound Matrix Rounding ([Ch 04](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd)), or Basis Poset Isotonic Cut ([Ch 24](../chapters/ch24-isotonic-regression-matroid-intersection-synthesis.qmd)). |
| **Strings & Substring Posets** | Choosing an antichain of mutually non-substring patterns; matching dictionary words along a text with overlap $\le k$; Hall's condition on character masks $2^{|\Sigma|}$. | **`#060`** (*CF 1009 G Allowed Letters*), **`#063`** (*CF 590 E Birthday*), **`#148`** (*CF 717 G Underfail*) | Aho–Corasick Poset + Dilworth Antichain ([Ch 08](../chapters/ch08-poset-dilworth-hall-flow-elimination.qmd)), or Interval Coverage Spine ([Ch 19](../chapters/ch19-k-interval-coverage-equation-difference-method.qmd)). |
| **1D Arrays, Intervals & Linear Inequalities** | $\sum_{j: i \in [s_j, t_j]} x_j \ge a_i$; sliding window of length $M$ has sum $\in [L, R]$; $L_p$ monotonicity $b_1 \le b_2 \le \dots \le b_n$ minimizing $\sum w_i |b_i - a_i|^p$; LIS removal. | **`#015`** (*P3308 LIS*), **`#021`** (*P2766*), **`#101`** (*BOI Sequence*), **`#145`** (*P3358*), **`#147`** (*BZOJ 1283*), **`#149`** (*P3980 志愿者招募*), **`#151`** (*NEERC Cat*), **`#184`** (*NOI 序列*), **`#188`** (*LOJ #3303*) | Consecutive Equation Differencing $\Delta_i = E_i - E_{i-1}$ ([Ch 19](../chapters/ch19-k-interval-coverage-equation-difference-method.qmd)), LP Duality ([Ch 21](../chapters/ch21-lp-duality-totally-unimodular-matrices-polymatroids.qmd)), or Coarea / Isotonic Cut ([Ch 13](../chapters/ch13-ishikawa-convex-penalties-coarea-parametric-cuts.qmd), [Ch 24](../chapters/ch24-isotonic-regression-matroid-intersection-synthesis.qmd)). |
| **Scheduling, Stock Trading & Resource Reuse** | Buying/selling 1 stock per day; $M$ chefs cooking $P$ dishes with cumulative waiting time; dirty napkins washed over $m$ or $n$ days; vegetables expiring at rate $x_i$. | **`#086`** (*CEOI Order*), **`#156`** (*P1251 餐巾计划*), **`#157`** (*P2053 修车*), **`#158`** (*P2050 美食节*), **`#177`** (*CF 865 D*), **`#181`** (*P3826 蔬菜*), **`#182`** (*CF 802 O*) | Reverse-position lazy MCMF ([Ch 20](../chapters/ch20-cycle-covers-dynamic-scheduling-resource-reuse-hubs.qmd)) when $N \le 800$, or Regret Greedy Heaps (`模拟费用流`, [Ch 23](../chapters/ch23-simulated-mcmf-regret-greedy-heap-segtree.qmd)) when $N \ge 10^5$. |
| **Combinatorial Games & Tournaments** | 2-player alternating token walk on a grid or sliding puzzle; maximizing 3-cycles in a round-robin tournament; sports league elimination feasibility. | **`#001`** (*SGU 326*), **`#047`** (*P4055 游戏*), **`#048`** (*P1971 兔兔与蛋蛋*), **`#139`** (*P4249 剪刀石头布*), **`#140`** (*CF 1264 E*), **`#141`** (*P4307 球队收益*) | Dulmage–Mendelsohn mandatory matching nodes ([Ch 06](../chapters/ch06-grid-parity-dulmage-mendelsohn-games.qmd)), or $\binom{n}{3} - \sum \binom{d_i}{2}$ convex degree splitting ([Ch 18](../chapters/ch18-convex-marginal-splitting-degree-penalties-tournaments.qmd)). |

## 4. The 64 Quarantined Problems (`R-01`–`R-64`) — Bare Templates, Duplicate Models, and Non-Flow Traps

To enforce the **No Boilerplate Library Code** and **Zero Magic Gadgets** mandates of our curriculum, 64 problems from the 320-problem research pool were quarantined from the primary chapter ladders (`#001`–`#192`). Every quarantined problem falls into one of three pedagogical categories:

1. **Category `Q-A` — Bare Solver Templates (`AGENTS.md` Exclusion)**: The input already specifies raw directed/undirected edges, capacities, lower bounds, or costs, testing only copy-pasted Dinic, MCMF, Hopcroft–Karp, or Edmonds' Blossom syntax with **zero modelling transformation**.
2. **Category `Q-B` — Structural Duplicates**: Classic problems whose exact English-to-graph compilation is strictly subsumed by a richer problem in `#001`–`#256` (e.g., `POJ 3041 Asteroids` is an unweighted subset of `UVA 11419 SAM I AM` `#035`, which additionally requires reconstructing the König vertex cover via alternating reachability).
3. **Category `Q-C` — Non-Flow Lookalike Decoys & NP-Hard Boundary Traps**: Problems that either (a) were historically misclassified in flow problem sets (most notoriously the 4 non-flow problems inside Chinese `网络流 24 题`) and are actually solved by **Bitmask BFS/Dijkstra**, **Layered Shortest Path**, or **Dynamic Programming**, or (b) cross a mathematical boundary (concave edge costs, 3D matching, non-bipartite supermodular penalties) that makes the flow compilation NP-hard.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Deep-Dive Audit: Why the 4 Classic Boundary Traps (R-61 to R-64) Break Network Flow"}
1. **Why Concave / Fixed-Charge Edge Costs (`R-61`) Fail MCMF (`FM-16`)**:
   Suppose transporting $f \ge 1$ units along edge $e$ costs $C(f) = 100 + 2f$ (a fixed opening fee of $100$ plus $2$ per unit), while $C(0) = 0$. The marginal increments are:

   $$
   \Delta_1 = C(1) - C(0) = 102, \qquad \Delta_2 = C(2) - C(1) = 2, \qquad \Delta_3 = 2, \dots
   $$

   Because $\Delta_1 > \Delta_2$, if you place two parallel arcs $e_1 = (\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 102)$ and $e_2 = (\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 2)$, any shortest-path augmentation in MCMF will greedily route flow along $e_2$ (cost $2$) **without ever saturating $e_1$ (cost $102$)**! Even worse, Fixed-Charge Network Flow subsumes the **Directed Steiner Tree** problem (send 1 unit to each terminal $t_i$, paying $F_e$ per used edge and $0$ per additional unit), which is NP-hard.
   - *When CAN a fixed setup cost be modelled?* Only when it is a **0-1 decision without volume conservation**, compiled as a **Maximum Weight Closure (`Ch 09`)** where selecting project $i$ forces paying fixed cost $F_j$ ($i \xrightarrow{\infty} j \xrightarrow{F_j} T$, as in `#069` *[六省联考2017] 寿司餐厅*).

2. **Why 3-Part Chaining $S \to X \to Y \to Z \to T$ (`R-62`) Fails 3D Matching (`FM-03`)**:
   Suppose valid triples are $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $(x_2, y_1, z_2)$. If you build directed edges $x_1 \to y_1$, $x_2 \to y_1$ and $y_1 \to z_1$, $y_1 \to z_2$ (even splitting $y_{1,\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} y_{1,\text{out}}$), a unit of flow from $x_1$ can enter $y_1$ and exit to $z_2$, hallucinating the invalid triple $(x_1, y_1, z_2)$! Flow networks are **memoryless** at intermediate vertices.
   - *When CAN a 3-layer hypergraph be solved?*
     - If every valid choice pairs one resource from $A$ and one from $B$ **independently** for a middle agent $G$ (i.e., $G_k$ is compatible with $A_i$ and independently compatible with $B_j$), place the agent in the middle: $A_i \to G_{k,\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} G_{k,\text{out}} \to B_j$ (`#017` *酒店之王*).
     - If $A \times B \times C \le 5000$ in a 3D grid cover, $\min(A,B,C) \le 17$: brute-force the $2^{\min}$ bitmask of slices in the shortest dimension and solve 2D König MVC on the other two (`#052` *[HNOI2013] 消毒*).

3. **Why Non-Bipartite Same-Color Penalties (`R-63`) Fail Min-Cut (`FM-08`, `FM-09`)**:
   Penalizing $x_u = x_v$ (or rewarding $x_u \neq x_v$) has $A = C(0,0) > 0, D = C(1,1) > 0, B = C = 0$, so $A + D > B + C$ (strictly supermodular). On a bipartite graph $V = L \cup R$, substituting $y_v = 1 - x_v$ for $v \in R$ converts $x_u \neq x_v$ into $x_u = y_v$ (submodular!). On a graph with an odd cycle (such as $K_3$), minimizing same-color edges is equivalent to **Maximum Cut**, which is APX-hard on general graphs (and solvable via dual matching only if planar).

4. **Why General 2-SAT (`R-64`) Is Not an $s$-$t$ Min-Cut (`FM-25`)**:
   In an $s$-$t$ cut, an $\infty$-capacity arc $u \xrightarrow{\infty} v$ encodes the implication $x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1$ (equivalently $\bar{x}_u \lor x_v$, a Horn / 2-monotone clause). A clause $(x_u \lor x_v)$ is $\bar{x}_u \implies x_v$, which requires flipping one variable ($y_u = 1 - x_u$). If the clause graph of $(x_u \lor x_v)$ and $(\bar{x}_u \lor \bar{x}_v)$ is **not bipartite**, no global variable flip can turn all clauses into $z_u \implies z_v$ Simultaneously! Thus pure feasibility of mixed 2-CNF clauses belongs to **Tarjan SCC (2-SAT)**, whereas weighted optimization of 2-CNF requires the conflict graph of same-polarity clauses to be bipartite (as rescued in Flagship Benchmark #3, `ARC 142 E Pairing Wizards` `#096`).
::::

## 5. Complete Pedagogical Audit of the Classic Chinese "24 Network Flow Problems" (`网络流 24 题`)

Compiled in the early 2000s for Chinese NOI/CTSC training and hosted on LibreOJ (`LOJ #6000`–`#6023`) and Luogu, the **"24 Network Flow Problems" (`网络流 24 题`)** is the single most famous problem collection in competitive programming flow literature. However, studying the raw list in numerical order without a pedagogical map is notoriously hazardous for two reasons:

1. **Four of the 24 Problems Are Not Network Flow Problems (`FM-25`)**: Because the list was originally assembled around *"Linear Programming and Network Flow"* broadly, four problems (`孤岛营救问题`, `汽车加油行驶问题`, `软件补丁问题`, and one variant slot) have **zero multi-unit flow conservation** and are actually solved by **Bitmask 0-1 BFS**, **Layered Fuel-State Dijkstra**, or **Bitmask Shortest Path**. Generations of students have wasted hours trying to force Dinic or MCMF onto bitmask state transitions!
2. **Seven Problems Are Bare Templates or Near-Identical Clones**: Problems like `分配问题` (`P4014`), `运输问题` (`P4015`), and `飞行员配对` (`P2756`) hand the bipartite graph directly to the solver, while `圆桌问题` (`P3254`) and `试题库问题` (`P2763`) are word-for-word isomorphic.

### 5.2 Forensic Deconstruction of the Non-Flow Impostors (`R-51`, `R-52`, `R-53`)

Why did these three problems appear in `网络流 24 题`, and how do you immediately recognize in a contest that Dinic / MCMF is the wrong tool?

1. **`R-51` — Luogu P4011 *孤岛营救问题* (Island Rescue, `24题 #14`)**:
   - *Statement*: An $N \times M$ grid ($N, M \le 10$) has walls, doors of types $1 \dots P$ ($P \le 10$), and keys of types $1 \dots P$ scattered on cells. Find the shortest time from $(1,1)$ to $(N,M)$.
   - *Why Network Flow Fails*: Once you pick up a key of type $k$, you retain that key **forever** and can open any number of type-$k$ doors. In a standard flow network, a unit of flow cannot "remember" which vertices it previously visited without expanding the vertex space by $2^P$. Once you expand the state space to $(r, c, \text{mask} \in [0, 2^P))$, you only need **1 path** of minimum length—which is a standard shortest-path problem, not a multi-unit flow problem!
   - *Correct Algorithm*: **0-1 BFS (or BFS)** on the layered state graph $(r, c, \text{mask})$ with $10 \times 10 \times 2^{10} \approx 10^5$ states in $O(NM 2^P)$ time.

2. **`R-52` — Luogu P4009 *汽车加油行驶问题* (Car Refueling, `24题 #13`)**:
   - *Statement*: Drive a single car from $(1,1)$ to $(N,N)$ ($N \le 100$) with fuel tank capacity $K \le 10$. Moving decreases fuel by $1$; moving left/up costs $B$; gas stations force refuel for $A$; building a new station costs $C + A$.
   - *Why Network Flow Is Redundant Overhead*: Although a single shortest path is technically a 1-unit min-cost flow ($\text{flow} = 1$), there are **no edge capacity bottlenecks** shared across multiple cars. Running SPFA/Dijkstra MCMF on $(r, c, k)$ with capacity $1$ does the exact same work as **1 run of Dijkstra** on the layered state graph $(r, c, k \in [0, K])$ with $100 \times 100 \times 11 = 1.1 \cdot 10^5$ states!

3. **`R-53` — Luogu P2761 *软件补丁问题* (Software Patches, `24题 #22`)**:
   - *Statement*: A program has $N \le 20$ bugs (initial mask $2^N - 1$). Each of $M \le 100$ patches requires certain bugs to be present ($B_1$) and absent ($B_2$), takes time $t_j$, and fixes subset $F_1$ while introducing subset $F_2$:

     $$
     \text{mask}_{\text{next}} = (\text{mask} \setminus F_1) \cup F_2
     $$

   - *Why Network Flow Fails*: Bitwise set-union and set-difference on $N$ coupled bits cannot be expressed as additive flow conservation $\sum f_{\text{in}} - \sum f_{\text{out}} = 0$ on $O(N)$ vertices. Instead, the state space is the $2^{20} \approx 10^6$ hypercube of bug masks, solved by **Dijkstra's Algorithm on $2^N$ states** from $\text{mask} = 2^N - 1$ to $\text{mask} = 0$.

## 7. Longitudinal "Revisited" Threads (`Rev-01`–`Rev-14`) & Multilingual Bibliography

### 7.1 Index of Longitudinal Scaling Threads (`Rev-01`–`Rev-14`)

Each thread below traces a single problem family across multiple chapters as the constraint scale ($N, M, V_{\max}$) grows by $10^2\times$ to $10^6\times$ (full proofs in [Capstone I: Grandmaster Synthesis Reserve](synthesis-reserve.qmd)):

| Thread Code | Anchor Problem (Early Chapter) | Advanced Evolution (Later Chapter) | What Structural Scaling Breaks & How It Is Rescued |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`Rev-01`** | **`#020`** *P2754 星际转移* ([Ch 03](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd), $T \le 50$) | **`#142`** *CF 1187 G Gang Up* ([Ch 18](../chapters/ch18-convex-marginal-splitting-degree-penalties-tournaments.qmd), $d \cdot k^2$ congestion) | Unweighted time-expanded layers $V \times T$ upgrade to convex marginal parallel arcs $(d, 3d, 5d\dots)$ per time-step. |
| **`Rev-02`** | **`#042`** *P3355 骑士共存* ([Ch 06](../chapters/ch06-grid-parity-dulmage-mendelsohn-games.qmd), $N \le 200$) | **`#081`** *ABC 193 F* ([Ch 11](../chapters/ch11-bipartite-variable-inversion-supermodular-rescue.qmd)) & **`#173`** *CF 793 G* ([Ch 22](../chapters/ch22-ds-accelerated-flow-graphs-blossom-matching.qmd), $N \le 10^4$) | Grid parity bipartite MIS evolves into checkerboard variable inversion (`燃やす埋める`) and persistent segment-tree range matching. |

| **`Rev-04`** | **`#058`** *P2765 魔术球* ([Ch 08](../chapters/ch08-poset-dilworth-hall-flow-elimination.qmd), disjoint DAG paths) | **`#061`** *P4298 祭祀* ([Ch 08](../chapters/ch08-poset-dilworth-hall-flow-elimination.qmd)) & **`#063`** *CF 590 E* ($N \le 750$, $\sum |S| \le 10^7$) | Disjoint path cover upgrades to transitive-closure Dilworth antichain reconstruction and Aho–Corasick fail-tree compression. |

### 7.2 Master Multilingual Bibliography (`[EN]`, `[ZH]`, `[JA]`)

- **`[EN]` Foundational Papers & Combinatorial Optimization Monographs**:
  1. **Ford, L. R., & Fulkerson, D. R. (1962)**. *Flows in Networks*. Princeton University Press. (Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem, augmenting paths, Dilworth's Theorem reduction, and matrix rounding).
  2. **Picard, J. C. (1976)**. *Maximal Closure of a Graph and Applications to Combinatorial Problems*. Management Science, 22(11), 1268–1272. (Foundation of Chapter 9 Project Selection).
  3. **Kolmogorov, V., & Zabih, R. (2004)**. *What Energy Functions Can Be Minimized via Graph Cuts?* IEEE TPAMI, 26(2), 147–159. (Submodularity necessity & sufficiency $A + D \le B + C$ in Chapter 10).
  4. **Ishikawa, H. (2003)**. *Exact Optimization for Markov Random Fields with Convex Priors*. IEEE TPAMI, 25(10), 1333–1336. (Multi-state unary chains and convex cross-edge compilation in Chapters 12–13).
  5. **Gallo, G., Grigoriadis, M. D., & Tarjan, R. E. (1989)**. *A Fast Parametric Maximum Flow Algorithm and Applications*. SIAM Journal on Computing, 18(1), 30–55. (Nested parametric cut envelopes in Chapters 13, 14, and 24).
  6. **Gomory, R. E., & Hu, T. C. (1961)** & **Gusfield, D. (1990)**. *Multi-Terminal Network Flows* / *Very Simple Methods for All Pairs Network Flow Analysis*. (Gomory–Hu cut trees in Chapter 16).
  7. **Edmonds, J. (1965 & 1970)**. *Paths, Trees, and Flowers* & *Submodular Functions, Matroids, and Certain Polyhedra*. (Blossom contraction in Chapter 22 and Matroid Intersection / Polymatroids in Chapters 21 & 24).

- **`[ZH]` Chinese National Training Team Papers (`国家集训队论文`) & Treatises**:
  1. **胡伯涛 (Hu Botao / Amber, 2007)**. 《最小割模型在信息学竞赛中的应用》 (*Applications of Minimum Cut Models in Olympiad in Informatics*). 2007 国家集训队论文. (Definitive Chinese treatise on Maximum Weight Closure, Maximum Density Subgraphs, degree regularization, and $M+1$ lexicographical cut scaling; Chapters 2, 9, 10, 14).
  2. **周冬 (Zhou Dong, 2009)**. 《浅谈平面图最小割》 (*On Minimum Cuts in Planar Graphs*). 2009 国家集训队论文. (Planar cycle–cut duality for `[BJWC2006] 狼抓兔子` and `[NOI2010] 海拔`; Chapter 15).
  3. **武森 (Wu Sen, 2008) & 营员交流资料**. 《流守恒差分建模法与线性规划对偶》 (*Consecutive Equation Differencing and LP Duality in `[NOI2008] 志愿者招募`*). (Algebraic equation differencing $\Delta_i = E_i - E_{i-1}$ and TU duality; Chapters 19 & 21).
  4. **陈胤伯 (Chen Yinbo, 2016) & 王钦石 (Wang Qinshi, 2012)**. 《一般图匹配与带花树算法》 & 《浅谈拟阵交叉在竞赛中的应用》. 国家集训队论文. (Edmonds' Blossom and Matroid Intersection; Chapters 22 & 24).
  5. **高睿泉 (Gao Ruiquan, 2018) & 兔队 / UOJ 模拟费用流综述 (2018–2019)**. 《浅谈模拟费用流》 (*Simulated Min-Cost Flow and Regret Greedy Heaps*). 国家集训队论文. (Formalization of `模拟费用流` for `UOJ #455 雪灾与外卖`, `ICPC WF 2018 Conquer the World`, and `[NOI2019] 序列`; Chapter 23).
  6. **高翊峰 (Gao Yifeng, 2020)**. 《保序回归问题及其在信息学竞赛中的应用》 (*Isotonic Regression in Olympiad in Informatics*). 2020 国家集训队论文. ($L_p$ Isotonic Regression via Parallel Binary Search and derivative threshold cuts for `[省选联考 2020] 魔法商店`; Chapter 24).

- **`[JA]` Japanese Competitive Programming Treatises (`燃やす埋める` / Project Selection)**:
  1. **noshi91 (2019)**. 『燃やす埋める問題（Project Selection Problem）の解説』 (*Comprehensive Treatise on Burn-or-Bury*). (Algebraic truth-table decomposition, Bipartite Variable Inversion, and multi-state chain reversal; Chapters 10–13).
  2. **maspy (maspypy, 2020–2023)**. 『最小カットと燃やす埋める』『LP双対とネットワークフロー』 (*Min-Cut & Burn-or-Bury; LP Duality & Network Flow*). (Coarea level-set threshold derivations for `AGC 038 F`, `ARC 107 F`, `ARC 142 E`, and `ARC 137 E`; Chapters 11–13, 21).
  3. **tatyam & AtCoder Official Editorials (`AGC 018 C`, `AGC 029 F`, `AGC 031 E`, `AGC 034 D`, `AGC 038 F`, `ARC 106 E`, `ARC 107 F`, `ARC 125 E`, `ARC 142 E`)**. (Canonical Japanese structural reductions across Parts II, III, V, and VI).
